notes.definition: Before protons, neutrons and electrons were discovered, scientists classified the elements by arranging them in order of their atomic weights. Mendeleev improved this by leaving gaps for undiscovered elements and changing the order where properties did not fit, and his correct predictions led to his table being accepted.
explanation: In the early 1800s chemists could measure the relative masses of atoms (atomic weights) but nobody knew that atoms contained protons, neutrons and electrons. The obvious way to organise the elements was therefore to list them in order of increasing atomic weight and look for patterns. Chemists had noticed that some elements, such as lithium, sodium and potassium, or chlorine, bromine and iodine, had very similar chemical properties and wanted a system that put these families together.

Early periodic tables were incomplete because many elements had not yet been discovered. When the known elements were placed strictly in order of atomic weight, some ended up in inappropriate groups. For example, in John Newlands' 'law of octaves' (1864) every eighth element was said to be similar. This worked for the lighter elements but broke down after calcium, and it forced some elements with very different properties into the same group, such as metals alongside non-metals. Because Newlands left no spaces, any newly discovered element could not fit, and his idea was not taken seriously at the time.

In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev overcame some of these problems. He arranged the elements broadly in order of atomic weight but put elements with similar properties in the same group. To make this work he did two things. First, he left gaps for elements he thought had not been discovered yet. Second, in some places he changed the order based on atomic weights. For example, tellurium has a higher atomic weight than iodine, but Mendeleev placed tellurium first so that iodine sat with chlorine and bromine, whose properties it matches.

Mendeleev used the gaps to make predictions. From the elements around each gap he predicted the properties of the missing element, such as its atomic weight, its density and the formula of its oxide. Elements with properties predicted by Mendeleev were later discovered and filled the gaps: gallium in 1875 and germanium in 1886. Germanium, which Mendeleev had called eka-silicon, had an atomic weight of about 72.6 (he predicted 72), and its oxide had the formula GeO₂ as he predicted. These successful predictions convinced other scientists that his table was correct.

This is a good example of how science works. A new idea is useful if it can be used to make predictions that can be tested. If the predictions are confirmed by experiment or observation, the idea is supported; if they are not, the idea must be changed or rejected. Mendeleev's predictions could have been shown to be wrong, but they turned out to be right, which strongly supported his periodic table.

Later discoveries about atomic structure explained Mendeleev's choices. In the early 20th century the proton was discovered, and the modern periodic table orders elements by atomic number (the number of protons). Knowledge of isotopes made it possible to explain why the order based on atomic weights was not always correct. Relative atomic mass is a weighted mean of the masses of an element's isotopes. Tellurium has 52 protons and iodine has 53, so tellurium does come first, but tellurium's most common isotopes contain many neutrons, which gives it a higher relative atomic mass. The same explains argon (39.9) coming before potassium (39.1).
keyFacts: Early scientists arranged elements in order of atomic weight because protons, neutrons and electrons had not been discovered.
Early periodic tables were incomplete, and some elements were placed in inappropriate groups when strict atomic weight order was followed.
Newlands' law of octaves (1864) worked only for the lighter elements and left no gaps.
Mendeleev (1869) left gaps for elements he thought had not yet been discovered.
Mendeleev changed the order of some elements (for example tellurium and iodine) so that elements with similar properties were in the same group.
Mendeleev predicted the properties of undiscovered elements, such as eka-silicon.
Gallium (1875) and germanium (1886) were discovered with properties matching Mendeleev's predictions, filling gaps.
The modern periodic table is arranged in order of atomic (proton) number.
Knowledge of isotopes explains why the order based on atomic weights is not always correct.
Testing predictions can support or refute a scientific idea.

keyTerms.definition: The historical name for relative atomic mass: the average mass of an element's atoms compared with other atoms. Early periodic tables were ordered by atomic weight.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. The modern periodic table is arranged in order of atomic number.
A vertical column of the periodic table containing elements with similar chemical properties.
A horizontal row of the periodic table.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
The weighted mean mass of the atoms of an element, taking into account the abundance of each isotope, compared with 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
Newlands' 1864 idea that every eighth element, in order of atomic weight, has similar properties. It only worked for the lighter elements.
Mendeleev's name for the undiscovered element below silicon. It was later discovered and named germanium.

workedExamples.title: Explaining a swapped pair
workedExamples.question: Tellurium (Te) has a relative atomic mass of 127.6 and iodine (I) has a relative atomic mass of 126.9. Explain why Mendeleev placed tellurium before iodine.
steps: Strict order of atomic weight would put iodine first and tellurium second.
That would put iodine in the same group as oxygen, sulfur and selenium, and tellurium in the same group as chlorine and bromine.
Iodine's properties are similar to chlorine and bromine (for example it forms compounds such as NaI, like NaCl and NaBr).
So Mendeleev swapped them so that each element was in the group with elements of similar properties.
workedExamples.answer: He placed elements with similar properties in the same group, so he swapped the order to put iodine with chlorine and bromine and tellurium with sulfur and selenium.

workedExamples.title: Explaining the swap using isotopes
workedExamples.question: Tellurium has 52 protons and iodine has 53 protons. Iodine has only one stable isotope, iodine-127. About two thirds of tellurium atoms are tellurium-128 or tellurium-130. Explain why tellurium has a higher relative atomic mass than iodine even though it comes first in the periodic table.
steps: The modern table is ordered by atomic number, so tellurium (52) correctly comes before iodine (53).
Relative atomic mass is a weighted mean of the masses of all an element's isotopes.
Iodine's relative atomic mass is close to 127 because it has one isotope.
Most tellurium atoms have mass numbers of 128 or 130, so they contain more neutrons, which pulls the mean mass above that of iodine.
workedExamples.answer: Tellurium has fewer protons, but its abundant isotopes contain many neutrons, so its weighted mean atomic mass (127.6) is higher than iodine's (126.9).

workedExamples.title: Using a successful prediction as evidence
workedExamples.question: Mendeleev predicted that eka-silicon would have an atomic weight of 72 and form an oxide with the formula XO₂. Germanium, discovered in 1886, has a relative atomic mass of 72.6 and forms GeO₂. Explain how this supported Mendeleev's periodic table.
steps: Mendeleev's table made a prediction that could be tested: an undiscovered element with particular properties should exist.
When germanium was discovered, its properties were measured.
The measured values (72.6 and GeO₂) closely matched the predictions (72 and XO₂).
A confirmed prediction is evidence that the idea behind it is correct.
workedExamples.answer: The prediction was tested and confirmed, so the evidence supported the idea that his arrangement, including the gaps, was correct, and scientists began to accept it.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think Mendeleev arranged the elements by atomic number.
misconceptions.right: In fact protons had not been discovered in 1869. Mendeleev used atomic weights, and atomic number ordering came in the 20th century.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the gaps in Mendeleev's table were mistakes or missing knowledge he could not fill.
misconceptions.right: In fact the gaps were deliberate. He left them for elements he predicted had not yet been discovered, and he predicted their properties.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think Mendeleev ignored atomic weights completely.
misconceptions.right: In fact he kept broadly to atomic weight order but changed the order in a few places where properties did not fit.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the tellurium and iodine swap was explained by measurement errors in atomic weights.
misconceptions.right: In fact the atomic weights were correct. The swap is explained by isotopes: tellurium has fewer protons but heavier isotopes, so a higher relative atomic mass.

realWorld: Gallium, one of Mendeleev's predicted elements, is now used in gallium arsenide and gallium nitride semiconductors in LEDs and mobile phones.
Germanium (eka-silicon) was used in some of the first transistors and is used today in fibre-optic cables and infrared lenses.
The way Mendeleev's table was accepted after testing predictions is the same process scientists use today, for example when a predicted particle is searched for in experiments.
examTips: When asked what Mendeleev did, give both actions: he left gaps for undiscovered elements and he changed the order of some elements based on their properties.
When asked why his table was accepted, link the discovery of elements (such as gallium or germanium) to his predictions being confirmed. Just saying 'elements were discovered' is not enough.
If asked why order by atomic weight is sometimes wrong, mention isotopes and that the modern table uses atomic (proton) number.
Read any data table carefully: questions often give predicted and measured values and ask you to evaluate how close they are.
summary: Early periodic tables ordered elements by atomic weight because subatomic particles were unknown.
Early tables were incomplete and put some elements in inappropriate groups.
Mendeleev left gaps and swapped some elements so that similar elements were grouped together.
Elements later discovered (gallium, germanium) matched his predictions, supporting his table.
Isotopes explain why atomic weight order is not always correct; the modern table uses atomic number.

flashcards.front: How did early scientists order the elements?
flashcards.back: In order of atomic weight (relative atomic mass).

flashcards.front: Why could early scientists not order elements by atomic number?
flashcards.back: Protons, neutrons and electrons had not been discovered.

flashcards.front: Give two problems with early periodic tables.
flashcards.back: They were incomplete, and some elements were placed in inappropriate groups when strict atomic weight order was followed.

flashcards.front: What was Newlands' law of octaves?
flashcards.back: The idea that every eighth element (in order of atomic weight) had similar properties. It only worked for the lighter elements.

flashcards.front: What two things did Mendeleev do to improve the periodic table?
flashcards.back: Left gaps for undiscovered elements and changed the order of some elements based on their properties.
For elements he thought had not been discovered yet. He predicted their properties.

flashcards.front: Which elements filled gaps in Mendeleev's table?
flashcards.back: For example gallium (1875) and germanium (1886, Mendeleev's eka-silicon).
Elements were discovered with properties that matched his predictions.

flashcards.front: Which pair of elements did Mendeleev swap in his table?
flashcards.back: Tellurium and iodine: Te (127.6) placed before I (126.9) so iodine was with chlorine and bromine.

flashcards.front: What is the modern periodic table ordered by?
What discovery explained why atomic weight order is sometimes wrong?
flashcards.back: Isotopes: an element can have a higher relative atomic mass because its isotopes have more neutrons.

flashcards.front: Why were the noble gases missing from Mendeleev's first table?
flashcards.back: They had not been discovered; they are unreactive so were hard to detect.

questions.question: Before protons, neutrons and electrons were discovered, how did scientists arrange the elements?
options: In order of number of outer shell electrons
In order of the date they were discovered
markScheme: 1 mark: in order of atomic weight
questions.explanation: Atomic weights could be measured in the 1800s. Atomic number and electron arrangements depend on subatomic particles, which had not been discovered.

questions.question: Why did Mendeleev leave gaps in his periodic table?
options: Because he had run out of space on the page
Because some elements were too reactive to be placed
For elements he thought had not yet been discovered
markScheme: 1 mark: for elements not yet discovered
questions.explanation: The gaps were deliberate. Mendeleev believed elements existed to fill them and predicted their properties.

questions.question: Which element was discovered after 1869 and filled a gap in Mendeleev's table?
markScheme: 1 mark: germanium
questions.explanation: Germanium was discovered in 1886 and matched Mendeleev's eka-silicon. Oxygen, sodium and iron were all known before 1869.

questions.question: The modern periodic table is arranged in order of:
markScheme: 1 mark: atomic number
questions.explanation: The modern table orders elements by atomic number (number of protons). Relative atomic mass order is nearly the same but not always.

questions.question: Which scientist is famous for leaving gaps in the periodic table and predicting the properties of missing elements?
markScheme: 1 mark: Mendeleev
questions.explanation: Mendeleev (1869) left gaps and made predictions. Newlands proposed the law of octaves, Dalton measured atomic weights, Rutherford worked on the nuclear model of the atom.

questions.question: In Mendeleev's periodic table, elements in the same group had:
options: been discovered by the same scientist
markScheme: 1 mark: similar chemical properties
questions.explanation: Mendeleev grouped elements by their properties. Their atomic weights differ, and neutrons were unknown in 1869.

questions.question: Some early periodic tables put elements into inappropriate groups. What was the main reason for this?
options: The elements were arranged by colour
Atomic numbers had been measured wrongly
A strict order of atomic weights was followed
markScheme: 1 mark: strict order of atomic weights followed
questions.explanation: Following atomic weights strictly forced some elements with different properties together. Early tables left no gaps, which was part of the problem, and atomic numbers were not known.

questions.question: Which discovery explained why ordering elements by atomic weight is not always correct?
markScheme: 1 mark: isotopes
questions.explanation: Isotopes have different numbers of neutrons, so an element with fewer protons can still have a higher relative atomic mass if its isotopes are heavy.

questions.question: Tellurium (Te = 127.6) is placed before iodine (I = 126.9) in the periodic table. Which statement explains this?
options: Mendeleev measured the atomic weights incorrectly
Tellurium atoms have fewer protons than iodine atoms, but tellurium's isotopes are heavier on average
Iodine atoms have fewer electrons than tellurium atoms
Tellurium is a metal and iodine is a non-metal
markScheme: 1 mark: Te has fewer protons but heavier isotopes
questions.explanation: Te has 52 protons and I has 53, so atomic number order puts Te first. Most Te atoms contain many neutrons, so its weighted mean mass is higher.

questions.question: Mendeleev predicted that eka-silicon would be in the same group as silicon. Silicon's oxide is SiO₂. What formula did he predict for the oxide of eka-silicon (X)?
markScheme: 1 mark: XO₂
questions.explanation: Elements in the same group form compounds with similar formulae, so he predicted XO₂. Germanium oxide is GeO₂, which confirmed the prediction.

questions.question: Which pair of neighbouring elements is NOT in order of increasing relative atomic mass in the modern periodic table?
markScheme: 1 mark: argon and potassium
questions.explanation: Argon comes before potassium although its relative atomic mass is higher. The other pairs are all in increasing order.

questions.question: The discovery of gallium with the properties Mendeleev predicted is described as evidence for his periodic table. Which statement best explains why?
options: Gallium was discovered by Mendeleev himself
It proved that atomic weights are always in the correct order
It showed that all the gaps had now been filled
A prediction made using his idea was tested and found to be correct
markScheme: 1 mark: a prediction was tested and confirmed
questions.explanation: Scientific ideas are supported when their predictions are tested and confirmed. Gallium was discovered by Lecoq de Boisbaudran, not Mendeleev, and other gaps remained.

questions.question: Mendeleev's 1869 table had no group for helium, neon and argon. What is the best explanation?
options: They were placed with the alkali metals
They had not been discovered, because they are unreactive and hard to detect
They do not have a relative atomic mass
markScheme: 1 mark: not yet discovered (unreactive)
questions.explanation: The noble gases are so unreactive that they were not found until the 1890s (argon in 1894). A whole new group was then added.

questions.question: State one thing Mendeleev did that overcame problems with earlier periodic tables.
markScheme: 1 mark: left gaps for undiscovered elements OR changed the order of some elements based on properties / did not strictly follow atomic weight
questions.explanation: Either of Mendeleev's two key changes earns the mark.

questions.question: Name the subatomic particle whose discovery allowed elements to be ordered by atomic number.
markScheme: 1 mark: proton
questions.explanation: Atomic number is the number of protons, so the modern ordering became possible once protons were discovered.

questions.question: Give two reasons why early periodic tables were not successful.
markScheme: 1 mark: incomplete / many elements not yet discovered (no gaps left for them)
1 mark: some elements placed in inappropriate groups / elements with different properties in the same group (because strict atomic weight order followed)
questions.explanation: These are the two problems the AQA specification identifies with early tables.

questions.question: Explain why scientists in the 1860s arranged elements by atomic weight rather than atomic number.
markScheme: 1 mark: protons / subatomic particles had not been discovered
1 mark: so atomic number was unknown, but atomic weights could be measured
questions.explanation: Atomic number is the number of protons; without knowing about protons, the only measurable ordering property was atomic weight.

questions.question: Iodine (126.9) has a lower relative atomic mass than tellurium (127.6). Explain why Mendeleev placed iodine after tellurium.
acceptedAnswers: properties more important than atomic weight
markScheme: 1 mark: iodine has similar (chemical) properties to chlorine and bromine / tellurium similar to sulfur and selenium
1 mark: so he changed the order to put elements with similar properties in the same group
questions.explanation: Mendeleev gave priority to properties over strict atomic weight order.

questions.question: Explain how the discovery of an element with properties predicted by Mendeleev provided evidence for his periodic table.
markScheme: 1 mark: Mendeleev used his table to predict the properties of an undiscovered element / a gap
1 mark: the element was discovered and its properties matched / the prediction was confirmed, supporting his idea
questions.explanation: A confirmed prediction is strong evidence: the idea could have been refuted but was not.

questions.question: Other scientists did not accept Mendeleev's table straight away. Suggest why, and state what made them change their minds.
markScheme: 1 mark: gaps / changing the order looked like he was adjusting the data to fit his idea / no evidence the missing elements existed
1 mark: elements such as gallium or germanium were discovered with the properties he predicted
questions.explanation: Until the predictions were confirmed, the gaps and swaps had no supporting evidence.

questions.question: Newlands arranged elements in order of atomic weight and said every eighth element had similar properties. Give one strength and one weakness of his idea.
markScheme: 1 mark (strength): recognised a repeating (periodic) pattern in properties / worked for the lighter elements
1 mark (weakness): broke down after calcium / left no gaps / put elements with very different properties in the same group
questions.explanation: Newlands spotted periodicity but his rigid pattern could not cope with undiscovered elements.

questions.question: Argon (39.9) comes before potassium (39.1) in the periodic table. Use their properties to explain why potassium belongs in Group 1 rather than with the noble gases.
markScheme: 1 mark: potassium is a reactive metal with properties similar to lithium and sodium (for example reacts with water)
1 mark: argon is an unreactive gas with properties similar to helium and neon
questions.explanation: Placing elements by properties puts K in Group 1 and Ar in Group 0, even though this reverses atomic weight order.

questions.question:
Tellurium has 52 protons and iodine has 53 protons. Iodine has one stable isotope, iodine-127. Most tellurium atoms are tellurium-128 or tellurium-130.
Explain why tellurium has a higher relative atomic mass than iodine but comes before iodine in the modern periodic table.
markScheme: 1 mark: the modern table is ordered by atomic number, and tellurium has fewer protons (52 v 53)
1 mark: relative atomic mass is a (weighted) mean of the masses of the isotopes
1 mark: most tellurium atoms have mass numbers above 127 / have more neutrons, so the mean is higher than iodine's
questions.explanation: Isotopes change mass without changing atomic number, which explains the swap Mendeleev made on the basis of properties.

questions.question:
Mendeleev's predictions for eka-silicon and the measured properties of germanium are shown.
Atomic weight: predicted 72, measured 72.6
Density: predicted 5.5 g/cm³, measured 5.3 g/cm³
Formula of oxide: predicted XO₂, measured GeO₂
Formula of chloride: predicted XCl₄, measured GeCl₄
Evaluate how accurate Mendeleev's predictions were.
markScheme: 1 mark: atomic weight very close (within about 1%)
1 mark: density close but slightly too high (about 4% out)
1 mark: conclusion: predictions were very accurate overall, and both formulae were exactly correct
questions.explanation: Good evaluation uses the data: 0.6 out of 72.6 is under 1%, 0.2 out of 5.3 is about 4%, and the formulae match exactly.

questions.question: Describe how the periodic table developed from the early tables of the 1800s to Mendeleev's table, and explain why Mendeleev's table came to be accepted.
markScheme: Indicative content: subatomic particles unknown, so early scientists ordered elements by atomic weight; early tables were incomplete because many elements were undiscovered; strict atomic weight order put some elements in inappropriate groups; Newlands' octaves worked only for lighter elements and left no gaps; Mendeleev (1869) grouped elements with similar properties; left gaps for undiscovered elements; changed the order of some elements (for example Te and I); predicted the properties of missing elements (for example eka-silicon); gallium and germanium were discovered with matching properties; confirmed predictions provided evidence, so scientists accepted the table.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a clear, logically ordered account covering the problems with early tables, both of Mendeleev's changes, and a linked explanation of acceptance via confirmed predictions.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes early tables and Mendeleev's changes, with a partial explanation of acceptance.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example 'Mendeleev left gaps', with little explanation.
questions.explanation: The best answers move in order: early approach and its problems, what Mendeleev did differently, then why the evidence (discovered elements matching predictions) led to acceptance.

questions.question: Explain how later discoveries about the structure of the atom explained the order of elements in Mendeleev's periodic table, including the positions of tellurium and iodine.
markScheme: Indicative content: protons discovered in the early 20th century; atomic number is the number of protons; elements in the modern table are in order of atomic number; this matches Mendeleev's order including the pairs he swapped; isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons; relative atomic mass is a weighted mean of isotope masses; tellurium has fewer protons (52) than iodine (53) but its abundant isotopes have more neutrons, so a higher relative atomic mass.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear explanation linking atomic number ordering and isotopes to the tellurium and iodine example.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): mentions protons or isotopes with limited explanation.
questions.explanation: Mendeleev ordered by properties where necessary; atomic structure later showed that properties follow atomic number, and isotopes explain the mismatches with atomic weight.

questions.question: Evaluate how well Mendeleev's periodic table meets the features of a good scientific idea. Use examples in your answer.
markScheme: Indicative content: a good scientific idea explains existing observations and makes testable predictions; it grouped elements with similar properties (for example Li, Na, K; Cl, Br, I), explaining known patterns; it allowed predictions of undiscovered elements (eka-aluminium, eka-silicon); the predictions could have been refuted but were confirmed by the discovery of gallium (1875) and germanium (1886), for example germanium's relative atomic mass 72.6 v predicted 72 and oxide GeO₂; limitations: some elements were out of atomic weight order (Te, I) with no explanation at the time; noble gases were missing; explanation came later with protons, atomic number and isotopes; it was able to be adapted (a new group added for the noble gases) rather than rejected; judgement: a strong idea because its predictions were confirmed.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed evaluation with examples of both strengths and limitations, and a reasoned judgement.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some strengths and/or limitations with at least one example, limited judgement.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple points about gaps or predictions with no evaluation.
questions.explanation: Evaluate questions need points on both sides and a conclusion. The key strength is that testable predictions were confirmed.
